clue.text: Sisterhood to which Judy and the C.O.'s wife belonged

definitions.text: Sisterhood to which Judy and the C.O.'s wife belonged

parts.words: Sisterhood to which Judy and the C.O.'s wife belonged
parts.note: Kipling's poem The Ladies ends 'the Colonel's Lady an' Judy O'Grady are sisters under their skins', so their sisterhood lies beneath the skin

explanation.surface: A society quiz asking which club a common girl and an officer's wife both joined.
explanation.walkthrough: C.O. is the commanding officer, Kipling's Colonel. The kinship the two women share is the one below the skin, which is the anatomical word for beneath the skin.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling's line makes the women sisters under the skin, and the medical adjective means lying beneath the skin.

clue.text: Context of apparent solar movement

definitions.meaning: the surroundings or background in which something is placed
the sun seems to sink below the horizon at evening

explanation.definitionFit: A background or environment is one sense; the other is the sun going down at dusk.

clue.text: He's in order to give a Unionist address

definitions.meaning: a monk or friar is a member of a religious order
trade unionists traditionally call one another by this word

explanation.definitionFit: A friar in a monastic order and a trade unionist greeting a comrade use the same title.

clue.text: Clears the Needles?

parts.note: the Needles are rocks off the Isle of Wight that a ship clears, but sewing needles are cleared by drawing out their cotton

explanation.walkthrough: The Needles are chalk stacks off the Isle of Wight on the English south coast that a ship must steer clear of; the needles here are for sewing.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking the cotton out of the eyes of needles leaves them empty, clearing them.

clue.text: Echo sounding like Richard

indicators.note: sounding signals that the phrase after it is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: like is AS, and Dick is the familiar form of Richard

explanation.surface: A voice that resembles someone called Richard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'like Richard' gives AS DICK, which sounds like ASDIC, the British wartime name for sonar, which detects submarines by echoes.
explanation.definitionFit: The submarine-detecting apparatus works by sending out pulses and listening for the returning reverberation.

clue.text: She clove to myrtle !

parts.note: a girl's name that is also the botanical genus of the clove tree, a member of the myrtle family

explanation.surface: A woman who stayed faithful to someone called Myrtle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clove' looks like the past tense of cleave, she stuck to Myrtle, but it is the spice tree, which was classed in this genus of the myrtle family; the genus name is also a woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The clove tree was classified under this myrtle-family genus, whose name is also a woman's given name.

clue.text: Full of energy but not dressed

definitions.meaning: tire is an old word for attire, so not tired is not clothed

explanation.definitionFit: Being fresh and unwearied is one sense; the other takes tire as an old word for clothe, so it means unclad.

clue.text: Was Gordon before Khartoum so lacking in colour ?

definitions.text: Was Gordon before Khartoum so lacking in colour

parts.words: Was Gordon before Khartoum so lacking in colour
parts.note: General Gordon earned the nickname 'Chinese Gordon' in China before dying at Khartoum, and a pale face lacks colour

explanation.surface: A question whether General Gordon looked pale before the siege of Khartoum.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Gordon was 'Chinese Gordon' after his service in China, long before Khartoum; pale and colourless, he would be the zinc-oxide pigment that artists use.
explanation.definitionFit: The zinc-oxide paint used by watercolourists shares a name with a pale Gordon in his China years.

clue.text: Firewalker in a hurry

definitions.meaning: someone treading over burning coals would have scorching soles

explanation.definitionFit: A firewalker's soles are literally scorched, and the idiom for rushing somewhere hastily uses the same pair of words.

clue.text: Lassie

parts.note: Lassie is the collie heroine of films and television, a celebrity canine performer rather than a Scottish girl

explanation.definitionFit: Lassie the collie was a famous canine film performer, and the phrase also names Sirius in the night sky.

clue.text: Completed the second hole

parts.note: not golf: made a hole through something for a second time, punched it again

explanation.surface: A golfer finishing the second hole on the course.
explanation.walkthrough: The golf picture misleads: the meaning is pierced again, as with a stamp sheet given a second row of holes.
explanation.definitionFit: Punching holes again through paper or stamps is to pierce it a second time.

clue.text: With whom Macheath would presumably not have been happy

definitions.text: With whom Macheath would presumably not have been happy

parts.words: With whom Macheath would presumably not have been happy
parts.note: in The Beggar's Opera Macheath sings 'How happy could I be with either, were t'other dear charmer away', so with no woman at all he would be unhappy

explanation.surface: A question about the highwayman hero of The Beggar's Opera and which of his loves would suit him.
explanation.walkthrough: Macheath's famous song says he could be happy with either of his two women; the clue asks for the opposite of 'either', with none of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Macheath declares he could be content with either sweetheart, so the opposite pronoun, meaning not one of the two, would leave him miserable.

clue.text: Mischievous trick that may cause a tumble

parts.note: may in the sense of being able to, as in 'it can happen'
to trip someone is to make them fall

explanation.surface: A prank that might send someone sprawling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that' is a link. A cantrip is a Scots word for a witch's spell or a piece of mischief.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots usage the word means a spell or a playful prank, a mischievous trick.

clue.text: Making rugs, a matter of taste

indicators.note: making here means working the following letters into something new, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Whether one weaves carpets is down to personal preference.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Making' rearranges RUGS and A. The definition is literal: sweetness is one of the tastes.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweetness is one of the basic tastes, and this sweetener is something perceived on the tongue.

clue.text: Talked of by some in March

definitions.text: Talked of by some in March

parts.words: Talked of by some in March
parts.note: the marching song The British Grenadiers opens 'Some talk of' a Macedonian conqueror 'and some of Hercules'

explanation.surface: Something discussed by a few people during the third month of the year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'March' looks like the month but is a military march: The British Grenadiers, a British regimental quick march, begins 'Some talk of' this conqueror.
explanation.definitionFit: The Macedonian king is the first hero named in the opening line of the Grenadiers' marching song.

clue.text: She-sinner, converted, shows saintly devotion

indicators.note: converted means changed into another form, so the letters are rearranged; it also suits a reformed sinner

explanation.walkthrough: 'converted' rearranges the letters of SHE-SINNER, nicely chosen for a sinner who repents.
explanation.definitionFit: Placing a relic in a shrine, or cherishing something as sacred, is an act of reverence towards the holy.

clue.text: Are they thrown up by the underground theatre?

definitions.text: Are they thrown up by the underground theatre?

parts.words: Are they thrown up by the underground theatre?
parts.note: a theatre's company is its cast, so the soil-dwellers' company leaves coiled heaps of earth on a lawn

explanation.surface: A question about what a subterranean playhouse might produce.
explanation.walkthrough: Earthworms push up little coils of excreted soil on lawns; the clue treats the worms as a theatre company, whose cast is also the word for those coils.
explanation.definitionFit: Earthworms leave coiled heaps of digested soil on the surface, which share their name with a theatre company's players.

clue.text: Give a rocket further test

definitions.meaning: a rocket is British slang for a severe telling-off

explanation.walkthrough: A 'rocket' is British slang for a stern scolding; the surface suggests testing a missile.
explanation.definitionFit: Rebuking someone sharply is one sense; the hyphenated reading means trying out once more.

clue.text: Make reductions at the T.U.C.

parts.note: the letters of the Trades Union Congress abbreviation are what one gets by writing a three-letter word for slice in the other direction

explanation.surface: Economies imposed at the headquarters of the trade union movement.
explanation.walkthrough: The T.U.C. is Britain's Trades Union Congress. The answer, read as an instruction, writes C-U-T backwards, giving T-U-C. 'at the' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Economising by trimming spending or staff is to reduce, the phrasal verb used of budgets.

clue.text: It provides sound information or aid

definitions.text: It provides sound information or aid

parts.words: It provides sound information or aid
parts.note: a wireless set brings news and music by sound alone, and is a help to ships and aircraft

explanation.surface: A description of something that gives audible news or help.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of 'or aid' also make the answer, though no word in the clue signals a rearrangement, so the clue reads best as a description of a wireless.
explanation.definitionFit: Broadcasting delivers news by sound, and wireless signals also guide ships and aircraft as navigational help.

clue.text: One of the languages of love ?

definitions.text: One of the languages of love

parts.words: One of the languages of love
parts.note: the Latin-descended tongues share a family name with amorous affairs

explanation.surface: A question about which tongue lovers speak.
explanation.walkthrough: French, Italian and Spanish belong to the family of languages descended from Latin, whose name is also the word for a love affair.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin-derived language family bears the same name as a love affair, so it is a language of love.

clue.text: Shows how one wipes the score-sheet clean

definitions.text: how one wipes the score-sheet clean
definitions.meaning: removing the notes from a musical score

explanation.definitionFit: To indicate or signify is one sense; the hyphenated reading strips musical notation from a page.

clue.text: Suggests motive and is backed up in Times, perhaps.

indicators.note: in signals that the backed letters sit inside the rearranged ones
perhaps signals that the word Times appears in some other order
backed means the word up is read the other way round

explanation.surface: A newspaper report hinting at why someone acted, and supporting it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backed' turns the little word round and 'in' sets it inside the rearrangement that 'perhaps' signals. 'and is' are links; Times is not the newspaper here, just letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To attribute a reason or blame to someone is to suggest a motive behind their action.

clue.text: Designation which carries a stigma

definitions.meaning: a formal title or form of address
in a flower the stalk of the pistil bears the pollen-receiving stigma at its tip

explanation.definitionFit: A formal title is one sense; in botany it is the slender pistil stalk topped by the pollen-catching tip.

clue.text: Country with a kind of football madness

parts.note: RU is rugby union, a code of football
mania is frenzy or madness

explanation.surface: A nation gripped by soccer fever.
explanation.walkthrough: RU stands for rugby union, one kind of football. The country is now usually spelt Romania.
explanation.definitionFit: The Balkan nation was commonly spelt this way in English in the mid-twentieth century.

clue.text: A stranger wedding-custom

parts.note: read 'stranger' as a noun: the custom of marrying a stranger, someone from outside one's own tribe or clan

explanation.walkthrough: 'stranger' looks like the comparative of strange, an odder custom, but it is the noun: the custom of marrying someone from outside the group.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthropologists use the term for the rule of marrying outside one's own clan, that is, an outsider.

clue.text: She was twice refused

parts.note: the 1925 musical comedy's title says 'No, No' to its heroine, two refusals before her name

explanation.surface: A woman turned down on two occasions.
explanation.walkthrough: The musical No, No, Nanette puts two refusals in front of the heroine's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of the musical comedy is named after a double 'no' in its title, so she is turned down twice.

clue.text: Throwing caution to winds, since Cape is said to be safe for shipping

indicators.note: is said signals that the safe-for-shipping word is only heard, not spelt as it sounds

parts.note: a coast free of wrecks would be wreck-less
a ness is a headland or cape, as in Loch Ness or Dungeness

explanation.surface: A rash act justified because a headland is reckoned harmless to vessels.
explanation.walkthrough: A headland with no shipwrecks would be wreck-less, a homophone of the rash adjective. 'since' and 'to be' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Throwing caution to the winds is acting with rashness and no regard for danger.
